abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeSamuel Johnson. Edited by John H. Middendorf The Lives of the Poets The Lives of the Poets. Samuel Johnson. Edited by John H. Middendorf. The Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson, vols. 21–23. Edited by Robert DeMaria Jr. New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, 2010. Pp. xii+1583.Anthony W. LeeAnthony W. LeeUniversity of Maryland University College Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreIn 1905, Clarendon Press published George Birbeck Hill’s three-volume edition of Samuel Johnson’s Lives of the English Poets. Few probably imagined at the time that this edition would hold sway for a full century. Shortly after the Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson commenced publication with its 1958 inaugural volume, Diaries, Prayers and Annals, many Johnson scholars shared the opinion of Albrecht B. Strauss, textual editor of the Yale Rambler, that a new edition of the Lives was just around the corner: “After an embarrassingly slow start the Edition is…finally underway, and subsequent volumes should appear in rapid succession. At least, one hopes so.”1 The check on Strauss’s cautious optimism registered by his ominously terse final sentence proved prophetic. It would be nearly half a century before the work that editor John H. Middendorf has called “arguably the most Johnsonian of Johnson’s works” and claimed as “the finest body of English literary criticism of the eighteenth century” (Yale Edition, 21:xii) would appear. After the resignation of two earlier editors, Frederick Hilles and William R. Keast, numerous delays and false starts—and most important, perhaps, the intervention of a rival edition in 2006, Roger Lonsdale’s Oxford Clarendon Press four-volume Lives—this year we finally have in our hands the Yale Lives.It is a lovely set. Each of the three volumes is roughly equal in length, and each sits comfortably in one’s hands. The Baskerville type and font set on a light cream, acid-free paper and the generously sized font make the text easy on the eye. Beneath the paper jackets, a bright teal cover replaces the dark blue of the earlier volumes in the Yale Edition. In these days of electronic publishing and financially straitened publishers, when rumors of the disappearance of the book periodically flourish, it is comforting for a bibliophile to handle a set prepared with such care and high standards as this one.The true beauty of these books, of course, lies inside the boards, in Johnson’s words and in how the editors have presented these words. The text is clean and authoritative; the introductions are at once compressed and weighty; the illustrations, while not lavish, are welcome; the annotation is restrained but helpful; and the index is both ample and accurate. It is a genuine tragedy that John H. Middendorf, who died in 2007, did not live to witness the publication of the sumptuous work to which he devoted most of his life. However, this edition is more than the work of just one man. Indeed, it is a collaborative venture in the best sense of the word. In addition to the foundational work of Keast and Hilles, handling of five of the Lives was farmed out to Stephen Fix (“Life of Milton”), J. A. V. Chapple (“Life of Dryden”), James L. Batterbsy (“Life of Addison”), James Gray (“Life of Savage”), and James E. May (“Life of Young”). Further, because Middendorf died before final copyediting and proofing took place, the current general editor of the Yale Edition, Robert DeMaria Jr., oversaw completion and publication of the manuscript, aided, as he remarks, by perhaps “the most distinguished team of proofreaders ever assembled,” including the contributing editors, Howard Weinbrot, O. M. Brack Jr., and James Engell, as well as Middendorf’s widow, Maureen MacGrogan (21:xviii).Close scrutiny of these volumes reveals that the accuracy of the text and annotation is high. Yet there is a reference to “Lives [1794]” (8 n. 6); I was unable to find a bibliographic reference to this tag in either the list of sigla (2) or within the list of Short Titles. And scholar James M. Osborn is misidentified as “John” in the title of the Festschrift compiled in honor of him (29 n. 3). Also, one feels at times that the annotation could be a bit fuller. For example, the reference to Cowley’s The Chronicle (51) does not receive a note but should. The editor at least tends to identify, if not fully explicate, Johnson’s references to specific passages from each author’s works; here he might have noted that the poem is a ballad from Cowley’s 1656 Miscellanies, one that, in the words of Mary Russell Mitford, “contains a catalogue of all the fair ladies with whom he [Cowley] had at different times been enamoured.”2 In the “Life of Shenstone,” Middendorf glosses Johnson’s mention of “the civilian’s gown” with a definition of “civilian” from Johnson’s Dictionary: “One that professes the knowledge of the old Roman law, and of general equity” (Yale Edition, 23:1343 n. 5). This is hardly sufficient—the note ignores the implied distinction among canon law, common law, and civil law that needs to be acknowledged and elaborated in order for the reader to thoroughly comprehend the reference. And when Johnson throws out a reference to Cowley’s “learned allusion” to “sepulchral lamps” (68), surely that deserves a note of identification.3 After all, not only seasoned scholars but also novice students will be expected to handle these volumes. In defense of these and other omissions, it needs to be said that the editorial policy of annotating the text rather than the topic perhaps demands such lacunae; such instances exemplify the limitations of the overarching policy (about which more in a moment) rather than those imposed by the editor himself.But it would be churlish to dwell on the petty blemishes of this splendid set, especially given their relative rarity. It is more gratifying to focus on its virtues, and perhaps the best way to do this is by comparing the Yale Lives with its great rival, Lonsdale’s Oxford edition. This inevitable comparison will allow the accomplishments of the Yale Lives with be set in a firmer context. Personally, I have been using Lonsdale’s edition practically every week over the past four years. Although I have been working with the present Yale Edition for only a few months, a number of useful reflections emerge from such a comparison.Had the Middendorf text been published five years ago, it would have triumphantly swept away all competition and claimed the laurel as the greatest modern edition of a Johnsonian work—high praise indeed. However, with the Oxford set occupying the field, this triumph is not quite so easily won. The principal differences between the two rest on the dual issues of text and annotation. The Yale Edition offers a greater—and more accurate—account of the textual history of the Lives. It uses as its copy-text the first edition of 1779–81; Lonsdale, however, chose for his the third edition of 1783. The Yale collation is more scrupulous and exhaustive than the Oxford effort; Lonsdale resists recording minor corrections and small variants, in order to avoid what he describes as a “massive amplification of the textual apparatus” (1:184). Also, in accordance with the editorial plan of the Yale Edition, its capitalization, possessives, and typography are modernized, whereas Lonsdale chooses not to attempt “to impose an artificial consistency on such aspects of the text” (1:184).What are some of the practical implications of these decisions for the user of these editions? In one sense, the Oxford text can be considered more authentic because it eschews any attempt at modernization. This was not the choice allotted the individual Yale editors, though—it was a top-down policy formulated by the general editorial board, a controversial decision that has been contested by many Johnson critics. However, given the focus on accuracy and the meticulous recording of variants by the Yale editors, their version must be considered perhaps more reliable, certainly more interesting, from a textual standpoint. But this emphasis in itself is not without problems, as a glance at the pages in of the Yale “Life of Pope” quickly shows. Because of the survival of manuscript and proof sheets of this Life, we have an unmatched window into Johnson’s compositional and revising modalities.4 However, in practical terms for users of the Yale Edition, this means putting up with textual notes that frequently erupt from the bottom margin of the page well into the space of the page itself, to say nothing of the numerous superscripted notes that thicket the text of Johnson’s prose at the top of each page. In this instance, Lonsdale’s choice of endnotes rather than footnotes seems a decided advantage, at least with regard to the recording of textual variants.The choice of copy-texts also affects the experience of the reader of these two editions. The Yale decision to opt for the first edition of the Prefaces, Biographical and Critical is the conservative choice. Following the Greg-Bowers tradition, this first edition represents a sounder decision because it is closer to the true state of the authorial handling of accidentals. Johnson himself was not attentive to such details and, hence, probably quietly allowed print-house emendations (as well as errors) to enter the text, so a strong case may be made for the first edition as the preferable copy-text. Yet, the third edition chosen by Lonsdale seems appropriate. Since it was the last version actively supervised (if that is the right word, given his typically lax editorial attention) by Johnson’s editorial guidance, it may be considered closest to his authorial intention—certainly in terms of substantive revisions. Most scholarly readers will probably prefer the conservative choice of the Yale editors as most sound.5 Even though Lonsdale uses the third edition for his copy-text, he nevertheless takes careful pains in his annotation to indicate emendations made by Johnson later in the compositional process. Likewise, the Yale editors record substantive emendations made to the text in their notes. For example, in the “Life of Dryden,” Lonsdale observes in both his general annotation and textual notes (2:218, 2:336–37) that Johnson made alterations to paragraph 154, regarding the details of Dryden’s unruly funeral. The Yale editors also observe this, in separate notes (both textual and annotative) on the same page (1:421). Hence, both editions do a good job of recording Johnson’s substantive emendations, albeit in a different fashion. Lonsdale’s method is less distracting; Middendorf’s method is fuller and more exhaustive.The second major difference in the two editions lies in annotation. Two opposing philosophies govern the two editions.6 The Yale Edition can be generally said to annotate the text, identifying quotations, allusions, and references. The Oxford edition, however, offers to annotate the topic as well as the text. That is to say, in addition to identifying works, authors, and events, Lonsdale expounds on the historical dimensions of the poets that Johnson discusses, as well as bringing in numerous Johnsonian and related literary and historical analogues. The results are strikingly different. Lonsdale’s annotation is massive, well nigh exhaustive, whereas Middendorf and his colleagues’ annotation is restrained and sparse. For example, in the “Life of Swift,” Lonsdale annotates paragraph 52 with a single note that almost engrosses two full pages of small-font print. During the course of this excursion, he ranges from a gloss on Hawkesworth’s edition of Swift’s works, to Swift’s correspondence and the Journal to Stella, to analogues in the “Life of Savage,” to the Rambler, to a conversation recorded in Boswell’s Life of Johnson, concluding with an informative mini-essay, replete with cross-references, on “subordination” (3:440–41). By contrast, Middendorf briefly references a remark of Johnson’s on subordination from Boswell’s Life, Gwin Kolb’s note on the topic in the Yale Rasselas, and Sir Joshua Reynolds’s Two Dialogues, In Imitation of Johnson’s Style of Conversation. In contrast to Lonsdale’s expansive cross-referencing, Middendorf laconically observes “for the nuances of SJ’s concept of subordination…see the many scattered references in the Life” (22:989 n. 2). This disparity is decisive. Sometimes, however—and more frequently than one might think—the Yale Edition admirably supplements Lonsdale. For example, in the “Life of Butler,” Johnson wraps up the biographical portion of this Life with the inclusion of John Barber’s Latin epitaph found on a monument in Westminster Abbey. Oddly, Lonsdale does not translate this lengthy inscription, unlike the Yale editors.The effect of these decisions is significant. The Yale Edition is easier to use—it is physically compact (three volumes vs. four, as well as being more compressed in length). Because the Yale edition uses footnotes rather than endnotes, less page thumbing is required. The Oxford Lives, while at times cumbersome—digging through the elaborate annotation can be quite time consuming, given the encyclopedic mass of information hoarded there—serves better as a reference work. If the corporate nature of the Yale Lives leads to greater accuracy and annotative reticence, the solo endeavor by Lonsdale (spanning a mere ten years, in comparison to the three decades plus required by the Yale Lives) is simply heroic, a monumental testament to the brilliance of one of the greatest scholars of our times.In the end, it is perhaps unfair to compare the Yale and Oxford editions. The Yale Edition is a magnificent achievement and deserves to be estimated and appreciated on its own terms. Its traversal from conception to publication has been a long, strange trip. But the result, for those of us left here to witness its arrival, is simply superb and compensates amply for our long wait. Notes 1Albrecht B. Strauss, “The Dull Duty of an Editor: On Editing the Text of Johnson’s Rambler,” Bookmark for the Friends of the University of North Carolina Library 35 (1965): 8–22, 9.2Mary Russell Mitford, Recollections of a Literary Life, quoted in Abraham Cowley: The Complete Works in Verse and Prose, ed. title: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667): A Seventeenth-Century English Poet Recovered . Eds. Michael Edson and Cedric D. Reverand II
abstract: As the above list shows, Abraham Cowley’s place in literary history has been a checkered one. In the 1660s, he was considered the greatest living English poet, and shortly after his death was ranked with Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton, and Dryden. However, literary tastes changed, and critics, readers, and fellow writers in the eighteenth century came to view his “extravagant” wit as exceeding the bounds of decorum and good taste. In the Epistle to Augustus, Pope echoes the lines by Addison, cited above: “Who now reads Cowley? If he pleases yet, / His moral pleases, not his pointed wit.” By the nineteenth century, Cowley fell off the map delineating the canon—a fall typically accompanied by the clichés of his unfashionable wit, some of which are rehearsed above. While he has had his advocates (see Miner, 1969, and Taafe, 1972, above) “the Cowley problem” (see Burrow, 2006) lingers. It is only somewhat lately, by fits and starts, that we find Cowley beginning to regain his footing upon the treacherous path of literary fame. (See the bibliographical list in the final note of the Introduction to Abraham Cowley [henceforth AC].) The present collection of essays is a major push forward in this effort. It does so, as the subtitle’s “recovered” intimates, not so much through a rehabilitation of Cowley as through attempting to rehabilitate his readers: “our contributors seek to recover what was always there.”The title of Cedric Reverand’s first chapter takes its cue from Pope: “‘Who Now Reads Cowley?’: How a Major Poet Disappeared from the Canon.” Like the beginning of Kevin Cope’s following chapter, Reverand seeks to account for Cowley’s disappearance from the foreground of literary history and absence within classroom texts and reading assignments. The suggested explanations are all plausible: the economic pressures of academic publishing, changes in literary taste, and what Reverand calls “category confusion”: the insistence that writers of the past be pigeonholed in neat categories and distinctly exact genealogies. In order for Cowley to be given proper due, he needs a modern bibliography and a critical edition. But this desideratum perhaps begs the question of justification: for what reason/s does Cowley deserve present and future scholarly attention? Furthermore, why is Cowley susceptible to “confusion”? Is it because, as T. S. Eliot suggests above (1938), he is a transitional poet, wandering between two worlds, one dying and the other struggling to be born? Unlike Dryden, who successfully navigated the shift, was Cowley born half a generation too soon? Or did he die too early, in 1667, at forty-nine, the year before Neander proclaimed a new literary age, in An Essay of Dramatick Poesie? Who can clear up this “confusion”?The editors of this book identify a specific explanation: “Cowley’s initial popularity and later disappearance had more to do with poetics than politics. In bridging disciplines (botany and poetry), modes (prose and verse), and genres (lyric, ode epic) in unexpected ways, Cowley’s poetry was challengingly experimental, either far ahead of its time or . . . ages behind it. We see Cowley as being ahead of everyone.” This proclamation also forms the overarching theme of the book: “The hybrid, experimental quality of Cowley’s poetry is one of the central issues, and a connecting theme, in the present collection.” If only for boldly facing such questions as these, the book is worthy of interest. And in the process of addressing and answering them, AC enhances our understanding of Cowley’s contribution to seventeenth-century poetry. Cowley has long deserved better than he has received; perhaps today his time has come?The phrase “hybrid, experimental quality” intrigues me. It is something that I have thought about quite a bit before reading this book. What does “hybrid” mean? The OED says: “Hybrid: Transf. and fig. “Anything derived from heterogeneous sources, or composed of different or incongruous elements; in Philol. a composite word formed of elements belonging to different languages.” The word was originally introduced into English by scientists, in the seventeenth century. Almost simultaneously, as a concept, it was also cultivated by authors for deployment in their literary works—notably during the very era when Cowley flourished. However, the scribes of some of the earliest texts recovered from ancient times cultivated it: according to the documentary hypothesis, at least three strands of the Book of Genesis, a foundational text in the Western tradition, were integrated into a whole during the post-exilic period. And so too with Homer. Classicists generally agree that the Iliad and the Odyssey were originally oral narratives, spoken to groups of listeners over several generations. It was only around the eighth century BCE that they were written down. In the swirl of the earlier transmissions, the Telemachy, the first four books of the Odyssey, were probably combined with an earlier “text.” Pindar too—a favorite of Cowley’s—may be said to be a hybrid author, in his mixture of praise for Olympic athletes with historical and mythic events, in his odes. Coming at this issue from different sources (see especially H. A. Mason’s two critical studies of 1959 and 1986), I use the terms “mosaic” and/or “tesseræ” to mean roughly the same thing as “hybrid”—that is, in the sense specifically denoted in the OED: “heterogeneous sources, or composed of different or incongruous elements” (my emphasis), that is, composed of multiple different ingredients. Today, “hybrid” has come to have the popular connotation of dyad, as in a hybrid car—a vehicle powered by gasoline and electricity; however, by noting the emphasis in the OED on the plural, “heterogeneous sources,” the three terms may be roughly considered synonyms. I have, for example, found numerous instances of small mosaics or hybrids studying the work of two later authors, Samuel Johnson and Thomas Carlyle.An example: In Book One of The Davideis, Cowley inserts a paraphrase of Psalm 114. He does so at the point where Saul’s frenzy is described: only “Davids Lyre [would] Sauls wild rage controul, / And tun’d the harsh disorders of his Soul.” Making its entrance here, the interpolation becomes the thing itself described, shifting from third person to first person, and hence modulating from the epic form to a dramatic episode. In a note, Cowley claims he is “inserting an Ode into an Heroick Poem” (Poems, 1656, 13–14, 37). Its presence thus creates a generic hybrid. The Psalm itself recounts the exodus from Egypt across the Jordan, thereby emphasizing the link between Moses and David as two of Israel’s greatest leaders (this in addition to the connection between David and Abraham enforced in Matthew 1:1–6 and developed elsewhere in Davideis). After the epic narrative resumes, Cowley quickly adds a brief paraphrase from another Psalm, 58: 4–5: “But Envys serpent still with him remain’’d / And the wise Charmers healthful voyce disdain’d.” Cowley’s ventriloquizing of David in the poem evokes a direct presence, as an actor on the stage. This is not “category confusion”: we rather witness here a hybridization of poetry (the body of the poem) and prose (the paratextual note): an event contributor Joshua Swidzinski denominates “prosimetric.” (The note itself contains a tag from Horace’s Ars poetica, and thus is itself an example of a smaller prosimetric instance nestled inside a much larger one.) The dimensions of this “mosaic” or “hybrid” constitute a deep moraine I have hardly begun to tap. Let it suffice to end by observing that an earlier epic poet quotes from Psalm 114 (113 in the Vulgate numbering): in Purgatorio 2:46–48, Dante has the pilgrims “singing all” “‘In exitu Israel de Aegypto,’” “with as much of that / psalm as is written thereafter” (Durling trans., 37).Reverand offers a fascinating alternative literary history to chart Cowley’s reputational demise. Tradition has held Samuel Johnson as the villain—particularly his seemingly atrabilious dismissal of the “metaphysical” school in his own favorite biography, the Life of Cowley. Reverand upends tradition by displacing blame from Johnson onto Eliot (see 1921 above). As I have argued elsewhere (Lee 2022, 2024) the latter’s critical pronouncements are more complex than scholars sometimes give him credit for. Tradition probably errs when crediting Johnson with naming this school; the keen reader will observe that he likely borrowed the term from Dryden (see 1693, above). For Reverand, it was Eliot’s dismissal—not Johnson’s purportedly crushing blow—that eclipsed interest in Cowley. This is fair. Reverand’s case is supported by a reading of several poems and an attentiveness to the publication of editions.The next chapter, Kevin Cope’s “Ease, Confidence, Difficulty, and Grasshoppers: Abraham Cowley’s Segmented Baroque,” identifies a new hermeneutical key to unlocking Cowley’s poetry. He defines his coinage, “segmented baroque,” thus: “Instead of unveiling stunning conceits and letting the reader quickly interpret them, and instead of writing discursive verses to elucidate the ideas he presents, Cowley continuously modifies images themselves, . . . so that they maintain a degree of baroque immediacy yet gradually disclose more information.” This notion of segmentation perhaps was inspired by Samuel Johnson’s remarks in his Life of Cowley: “Their attempts were always analytick; they broke every image into fragments: and could no more represent, by their slender conceits and laboured particularities, the prospects of nature, or the scenes of life, than he, who dissects a sun-beam with a prism can exhibit the wide effulgence of a summer noon” (Lives of the English Poets, 1:201). Cope’s novelty, however, consists in discerning in these “analytick fragments” the seeds of development for additional, related ideas in a sequential pattern of unfolding. Instead of possessing a discrete, gem-like integrity, self-contained, as may often be found in Donne’s or Herbert’s images, Cope argues, Cowley’s are linked on a chain, like a necklace, except that each new gem on the strand differs from and yet is an extension of its preceding neighbor.Take for example the third and fourth stanzas of “Hymn. To Light” (Cope quotes and analyzes three through six):Hail active Natures watchful Life and Health Her Joy, her Ornament, and Wealth! Hail to thy Husband Heat, and Thee!Thou the Worlds beauteous Bride, the lusty Bridegroom He!Say from what Golden Quivers of the Sky Do all thy winged Arrows fly? Swiftness and Power by Birth are thine:From thy great Sire they came, thy Sire the word Divine.For Cope, the “Light” of the poem is not an object in itself but rather the means by which things are perceived—a mode of apprehension rather than a scientific inquiry as found, for example, later in Newton and Goethe. And so, from this foundation issues a series of reflected perceptions: a personification of marriage with Heat, a quiver, then swift arrows, and the additionally approximated dispositions in stanzas five and six. Cowley is thus “difficult” in his poem’s operative conceit, yet “easy” as its gentle forward momentum encourages the reader’s ready comprehension.Following Cope, we arrive at a poetics that articulates an initial thought or image, and then traces it across a segmented series of tactical maneuvers: a congeries of “incomplete, partially explored viewpoints—which cross-sects, bisects, dissects, and in sum insects” (the latter a pun relying upon the connotation of the tripartite structure of abdomen, thorax, and head—cleverly deploying the noun “insect” as a verb). This method arrives at an understanding of the whole that accounts for each “bead” along the way. These beads are not fractals, rather the sum of the parts becomes greater than the whole. And often, the linkage moves from large to small or small to large. Joseph Addison discussed this in 1712, when reflecting upon the telescope and microscope and the great chain of being that it revealed:Here Addison is describing the great chain of being, just as the “Hymn,” which patterns the Chain’s movement from large to small. It begins with an enormous, universal phenomenon, light, then moving to the Empedoclean element of fire—a building block of the universe. The poem turns from cosmic to human, the marriage of male and female, and then to a smaller aspect of the human world, a container, the quiver, and its occupants, arrows: a move that not coincidentally poises marital love and harmony against hatred and battle. Probing the texture of Cowley’s poetry in this manner suggests that it possesses a dynamic complexity not unlike that found in Pope.By “Baroque” Cope intends the poetic complications found in Crashaw, Cleveland, Donne, and their Continental precursor, Giambattista Marino (1596–1625). Reverand prefers the term “mannerist” for the Metaphysicals, “because of the cynicism, irony, paradox, strained metaphors, bizarre situations, and unresolved contradictions in their poetry.” I hesitate to use the term neoclassic, because of the diffusiveness of sweeping periodization; nevertheless, might I suggest extending Cope’s hermeneutic protocol to “Neoclassic segmentation,” as found, for example, in Dryden’s Annus Mirabilis (published the year of Cowley’s death, 1667):The diligence of Trades and noiseful gain, And luxury, more late, asleep were laid:All was the night’s; and in her silent reign, No sound the rest of Nature did invade.In this deep quiet, from what source unknown, Those seeds of fire their fatal birth disclose:And first few scatt’ring sparks about were blown, Big with the flames that to our ruine rose.Then in some close-pent room it crept along, as it in with boldly with like some or great for which he with for new does And the to him with the fire his And small into the his And him to his first like His flames from but to every he is than now no of his He up at it with the with a wide And at every his of from the to the fire into a they And their with describing the of the of upon the image of rather than Cowley’s the segmentation The initial describing the of the the sparks as seeds which into an a of the a who his by and by of the past a at the of and were as the of in the century, some on and a and Dryden’s as is and Its are in stanzas and unlike the at times of Cowley’s each of Dryden’s its own thus him the extension to dimensions of the or Like “Hymn,” the Annus of the great chain of being, unlike Dryden’s the of or a by an greater to small.
